incidente.resumo: After an upgrade of the operator's reservation/check-in system, a programming flaw treated adult female passengers with the title 'Miss' as children, allocating them 35 kg instead of 69 kg; with 38 females misidentified, the load sheet for G-TAWG's departure from Birmingham on 21 July 2020 understated takeoff mass by 1,244 kg. The flight continued normally and the AAIB found safe operation was not compromised; the text does not describe any action that ended the event, only subsequent safety actions.
servicos_afetados: G-TAWG flight from Birmingham to Palma de Mallorca

descricao.texto: On the first flight after the upgraded system was implemented, the flight dispatcher and the operator's systems delivery manager spotted an adult female passenger checked in and shown on the load sheet as a child; a check of that flight revealed two other cases.
trechos:
On the first flight after the upgraded system was implemented, an adult female passenger
was checked in for a flight as a child and was also shown on the load sheet as a child.

This
was spotted by the flight dispatcher and the operator’s systems delivery manager.

A check
of the flight revealed two other cases where the same error had occurred.

descricao.texto: A flaw in the programming of the upgraded IT system interpreted the title 'Miss' as a child rather than an adult female, because in the country where the system was programmed Miss denotes a child and Ms an adult female; affected passengers were allocated a child's standard weight of 35 kg instead of 69 kg, and with 38 females misidentified the load sheet takeoff mass was 1,244 kg below the actual mass.
trechos:
The incident occurred due to a simple flaw in the programming of the IT system, which was
due to the meaning of the title ‘Miss’ being interpreted by the system as a child and not an
adult female.

This was because in the country where the system was programmed, Miss is
a child and Ms is an adult female.

The system allocated them a child’s standard weight of 35 kg as opposed
to the correct female standard weight of 69 kg.

Consequently, with 38 females checked in
incorrectly and misidentified as children, the G-TAWG takeoff mass from the load sheet was
1,244 kg below the actual mass of the aircraft.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: The relationship between passenger title and allocated standard weight was not discussed before the upgrade, and no specific test scenarios looking at passenger titles were examined in User Acceptance Testing; the issue was not identified in the initial risk analysis.
trechos:
The relationship between a passenger’s
title and the standard weight allocated was not discussed.

No specific test scenarios looking
at passenger titles were examined in the UAT.

This issue had not been identified as part of the initial risk
analysis and did not manifest itself during the trial simulations.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: The manual correction of adult females listed as 'Miss' was handled by teams that did not work over the weekend, and online check-in opened 24 hours before the flight on Monday 20 July, so the incorrectly allocated passenger weights were not corrected.
trechos:
A combination of the teams not working over the weekend and the ‘online’ check-in being
open early on Monday 20 July, 24 hours ahead of the flight, meant the incorrectly allocated
passenger weights were not corrected.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: The software adaptation implemented on 17 July 2020 to change adult females from Miss to Ms automatically could only change bookings before check-in; bookings already checked in, including online up to 24 hours before departure, were not amended.
trechos:
The upgrade programmers adapted a piece of software, which changed the title of any adult
female from Miss to Ms automatically, and this was implemented on 17 July 2020.

This
adaptation was only capable of changing bookings before check-in.

Any passenger bookings
with the title Miss already checked in, including online up to 24 hours before departure,
would not be amended.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: On 20 July 2020 a software 'fix' was being applied to the system, which the report says was possibly preventing it from identifying incorrect passenger status before the incident flight.
trechos:
On this day, a software ‘fix’ was being applied to the
system, possibly preventing it from identifying incorrect passenger status before the incident
flight on 21 July.

Passengers were able to check in online 24 hours
before departure, on 20 July 2020.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: The flight crew noticed the load sheet showed 1,606 kg less than the flight plan and 65 children versus 29 expected; the commander considered the number high but plausible, and the crew accepted the load sheet. The 1,244 kg discrepancy exceeded the 500 kg last-minute-change threshold above which a new load sheet should have been produced, had it been identified.
trechos:
They noticed that there was a discrepancy, with the load sheet
showing 1,606 kg less than the flight plan.

They noted that the number of children shown on
the load sheet was higher than expected, at 65, compared to the 29 which were expected on
the flight plan.

The commander recalled thinking that the number was high but plausible; he
had experienced changing loads on the run-up to the temporary grounding1 as passengers
cancelled and altered trips at short notice.

After a brief discussion, the flight crew decided that they were
content with the load sheet, the actual bag weights being very close to standard and the
new ZFW being understood as a function of the differing passenger load.

For the incident flight, the
weight of passengers on the load sheet was below the actual weight of the passengers by
1,244 kg, which was more than the 500 kg LMC weight difference above which a new load
sheet should have been produced, had the weight discrepancy been identified.

descricao.texto: Prior to the incident flight, the reservation system from which the load sheet was produced had been upgraded; the operator's integrated check-in system was undergoing an upgrade as part of a wider system upgrade for the airline industry.
trechos:
prior to the incident flight the reservation system from which the load sheet was produced
had been upgraded.

Part of the operator’s IT system was an integrated check-in system, which was undergoing
an upgrade as part of a wider system upgrade for the airline industry.

acoes.texto: Already done: a member of the Systems team manually checked the flights daily to ensure the title 'Miss' was amended to 'Ms'.
trechos:
A member of the Systems team manually checked the flights daily to ensure
           that the title ‘Miss’ was amended to ‘Ms’.

acoes.texto: Already done: a secondary check was instigated with the Operations department against the booked passenger loads.
trechos:
A secondary check was instigated with the Operations department against
         the booked passenger loads.

acoes.texto: Already done: a reminder briefing was given to Ground Handling Agents to be alert at check-in or boarding for adult female passengers showing as Miss or a child.
trechos:
A reminder briefing was given to Ground Handling Agents to ask them to
        be alert at check-in or during boarding for any adult female passengers
        showing as Miss or a child.

acoes.texto: Already done: a formalised procedure for a Customer Care Executive to check bookings was instituted on 24 July 2020.
trechos:
A formalised procedure for a Customer Care Executive to check bookings
       was instituted on 24 July 2020.

acoes.texto: Already done: an upgrade of the system producing load sheets was carried out to prevent reoccurrence.
trechos:
An upgrade of the system
producing load sheets was carried out to prevent reoccurrence.

observacoes: Source is an AAIB bulletin (investigating body). The text says that before the incident flight the operator had applied interim measures (a manual Miss-to-Ms correction process, a request to check-in staff, and an automatic title-changing adaptation on 17 July 2020); these preceded the incident flight and did not restore anything during it, so they are not listed as mitigation. The report states the thrust used (88.3% N1) was marginally more than that required for the actual takeoff weight (88.2% N1), so safe operation was not compromised. Two other flights by the same operator departed the same day with inaccurate load sheets from the same issue. No safety or ground operations reports were submitted about the first occurrence on the first flight after the upgrade. The report does not say this delayed detection.
